# Tracing where a value came from and what it fed

The lineage routes walk a run backward to what fed it and forward to what it
fed, and let an operator start from a claim handle, a source, or a producer
instead of a run id.

## The template

A producing node holds a claim and fans out over two partitions; a consuming
node substitutes an attribute from it. One run leaves one claim split into two
sub-claims and two runs joined by a substitution.

```yaml
name: lineage-demo
version: "1"
messages:
  - type: ops/kick
nodes:
  - type: producer
    executor: verifier-shape-checks
    subscribes:
      - node: ops/kick
        type: terminal/success
        force_upstream_refresh: false
    claim_producers:
      - name: claim-producer-filesystem
        selector: data
        intent: rw
        alias: parent
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: give_up}
    fan_out:
      claim: parent
      partition_request: '{"list":[{"key":"p1"},{"key":"p2"}]}'
      parallelism: 1
      error_policy:
        kind: strict
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          checks:
            type: array
            default:
              - kind: row_count_absolute
                config: {min: 0}
          verifier_rows: {type: integer, default: 0}

  - type: consumer
    kind: attribute_passthrough
    subscribes:
      - node: producer
        type: terminal/success
        force_upstream_refresh: false
      - node: producer
        type: attribute/verifier_rows/changed
        force_upstream_refresh: false
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          seen:
            type: integer
            source: "{{nodes.producer.attribute.verifier_rows}}"
```

## Start from a source

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/by-source/attribute/verifier_rows"
```

The answer is the consuming node's lineage record. Its `substitution_refs` name
the upstream producing run. "Where did this value come from" is a single read,
not a scan.

## Walk a run both ways

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/runs/$CONSUMER_RUN"
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/runs/$CONSUMER_RUN/ancestors"
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/runs/$PRODUCER_RUN/descendants"
```

Reading the run by id returns its lineage record. Walking backward reaches the
producing run; walking the producing run forward reaches the consuming run. The
trace closes in both directions on the same pair.

Depth is the caller's to choose:

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/runs/$CONSUMER_RUN/ancestors?depth=1"
```

The answer reports the depth it honoured.

A run id with no lineage answers 404, so an operator can tell "nothing recorded"
from "nothing upstream".

## Start from an upstream run

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/by-source/run/$PRODUCER_RUN"
```

Returns the consuming run's record — the same relationship the forward walk
resolves, reached from the other end.

## Start from a producer

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/by-producer/claim-producer-filesystem"
```

Returns every claim record that producer committed. A producer that committed
nothing returns none rather than an error, so an empty answer is meaningful.

## Start from a claim handle

```bash
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/claims/$CLAIM_HANDLE_ID"
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/claims/$CLAIM_HANDLE_ID/descendants"
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/lineage/claims/$SUB_CLAIM_HANDLE_ID/ancestors"
```

The claim record carries the name of the producer that committed it and the
outcome it settled at. Walking it forward reaches both sub-claims the fan-out
created; walking a sub-claim backward reaches the claim it was split from.

The claim is a first-class entry point into the trace, not only something a run
record mentions in passing.
